title: LSQCA: Resource-Efficient Load/Store Architecture for Limited-Scale Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
problem: Current fault-tolerant quantum computer (FTQC) floorplan strategies devote 50% of qubit memory space to routing/overhead required for unit-time random access to all logical qubits, leaving only half the qubit count available for data storage when qubits are scarce.
method: LSQCA (Load/Store Quantum Computer Architecture) separates logical qubit memory into Computational Registers (CR), a small fast-access region, and Scan-Access Memory (SAM), a dense storage region accessed with variable latency. An instruction set is defined over these abstractions, with concrete implementations as point-SAM and line-SAM architectures. Access latency in SAM is hidden by overlapping it with other computational bottlenecks, exploiting access locality patterns identified through static analysis of quantum program memory reference timestamps. Optimization techniques leverage locality in memory reference ordering to further reduce effective latency penalties.

title: LUT-DLA: Lookup Table as Efficient Extreme Low-Bit Deep Learning Accelerator
problem: Scalar quantization cannot reduce DNN bit-width below 1-bit, capping compression gains; existing accelerators lack hardware support for vector-quantization-based LUT approaches that could push beyond this limit.
method: LUT-DLA converts DNN weight tensors into lookup tables via vector quantization, replacing multiply-accumulate operations with LUT index lookups and accumulations. The LUTBoost algorithm trains DNNs through a multistage process to learn LUT-compatible vector codebooks. A co-design space exploration framework evaluates the trade-off between LUT table size, codebook dimensionality, model accuracy, and hardware cost to select optimal hardware configurations. The ASIC accelerator implements LUT fetch-and-accumulate dataflow units that directly consume quantized indices to perform inference.

title: Pave: Information Flow Control for Privacy-preserving Online Data Processing Services
problem: When users submit personal data to remote online services for processing, they have no technical guarantee that the service will not leak their data, because the processing logic runs in an untrusted server environment entirely outside the user's control.
method: Pave provides a sandboxed execution environment (PaveBox) for arbitrary data-processing programs on a remote server. PaveBox, built on Intel SGX (a hardware trusted execution environment), intercepts all data flows into and out of the sandbox using a runtime monitor that applies information flow control (IFC) policies. Allowed flows are permitted without interference to preserve program functionality; disallowed flows (those that would expose user data) are blocked. Users can verify PaveBox's integrity and confidentiality via SGX remote attestation. The system's security is formalized in a model and proved, with quantitative analysis via prototype experiments.

title: CIPHERMATCH: Accelerating Homomorphic Encryption-Based String Matching via Memory-Efficient Data Packing and In-Flash Processing
problem: Homomorphic encryption (HE)-based exact string matching incurs prohibitive computational latency due to expensive HE operations (multiplication, rotation) and severe data movement overhead from the large ciphertext memory footprint. Prior HE string matching algorithms cannot efficiently handle these combined bottlenecks.
method: CIPHERMATCH is an algorithm-hardware co-design that (1) applies an optimized software-based data packing scheme to reduce ciphertext memory footprint, (2) reformulates the string matching algorithm to eliminate costly HE multiplications and rotations, replacing them with cheaper addition-only operations, and (3) introduces a new in-flash processing (IFP) architecture that performs computation near the flash storage to minimize data movement between memory and processor.

title: Accelerating Number Theoretic Transform with Multi-GPU Systems for Efficient Zero Knowledge Proof
problem: Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), a key bottleneck in zero-knowledge proof generation, has not been efficiently parallelized across multiple GPUs because its butterfly permutation access pattern generates high inter-GPU communication overhead that offsets the compute gains from additional GPUs.
method: The paper redesigns the NTT algorithm for multi-GPU execution by restructuring the butterfly computation stages to localize data access within GPU memory and minimize the frequency and volume of inter-GPU data transfers. The approach introduces a GPU-topology-aware permutation schedule that maps NTT stages to GPU assignments so that communication-intensive permutation steps are batched and overlap-optimized with computation. NVLink or PCIe interconnect topology is leveraged to select inter-GPU transfer paths that maximize aggregate bandwidth.

title: TransFusion: End-to-End Transformer Acceleration via Graph Fusion and Pipelining
problem: Transformer acceleration has focused on fusing individual submodules (MHA, softmax) in isolation, but as models grow in depth and context length, inter-layer data movement, buffer fragmentation, and scheduling inefficiencies across the full encoder/decoder stack (QKV projections, MHA, LayerNorm, FFN) dominate end-to-end latency and cannot be addressed by fragmented per-module optimizations.
method: TransFusion represents the full Transformer layer stack as Einsum Cascades — a structured DAG of Einsum operations capturing precise data dependencies and execution order. The DPipe scheduler partitions this Einsum DAG and applies latency-aware inter-layer pipelining across hardware memory hierarchies using dynamic programming to balance FFN and attention stages. TileSeek, a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based tiling search algorithm, explores the tile configuration space to balance buffer reuse against on-chip memory constraints at both cloud and edge scales.

title: FAST: An FHE Accelerator for Scalable-parallelism with Tunable-bit
problem: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) imposes enormous computational overhead compared to plaintext computation, and existing FHE accelerators do not exploit recent cryptographic optimizations—specifically hoisting technology and the gadget decomposition key-switching (KLSS) method—leaving significant performance on the table. Additionally, ciphertext level consumption varies significantly during application execution, causing workload imbalance that accelerators with fixed precision do not address.
method: FAST is an FHE accelerator that integrates hoisting technology (reducing redundant NTT operations in key-switching) and the KLSS gadget decomposition key-switching method. A versatile framework supports both hybrid and KLSS key-switching within a single application execution, dynamically adapting to varying ciphertext levels. The accelerator implements tunable-bit arithmetic to match the differing computational precision requirements of hybrid vs. KLSS key-switching at different ciphertext levels. Scalable parallelism is achieved through a configurable array of processing elements that can be provisioned to match the current workload's level and method requirements.

title: Clearance-Constrained PCB Global Placement with Heterogeneous Components
problem: PCB placement must handle pad-to-pad clearance constraints and heterogeneous components while minimizing routing congestion and overlap.
method: PCB placement framework with: wire-area model accounting for routing resource needs (power/signal nets); pad-to-pad clearance model; two-sided density model for component and pad overlap; quadratic programming-based legalizer resolving violations.

title: SMX: Heterogeneous Architecture for Universal Sequence Alignment Acceleration
problem: Sequence alignment accelerators are over-specialized to one alignment model (e.g., Smith-Waterman with affine gaps or simple substitution matrices) and fail to support the full variety of irregular use cases in practice (DNA, protein, ASCII text; weighted gaps; diverse substitution matrices), while general-purpose CPUs and GPUs lack the efficiency of domain-specific designs.
method: SMX is a heterogeneous architecture that integrates two components orchestrated by a general-purpose core: an ISA extension (SMX-1D) for irregular and sequential alignment tasks, and a specialized 2D coprocessor (SMX-2D) to accelerate the regular, parallel compute-intensive phases of dynamic programming. The ISA extension adds new instructions to handle variable-length sequences and edge cases, while the coprocessor accelerates the systolic-style inner-loop wavefront computation. Both components support multiple sequence types (DNA, protein, ASCII) and alignment models including weighted affine gap penalties and full substitution matrices, enabling seamless integration with state-of-the-art software alignment algorithms. Physical design targets a 22nm technology node with an area of 0.34mm², 30% of a single-issue in-order CPU core.

title: Velosiraptor: Code Synthesis for Memory Translation
problem: OS code for configuring hardware memory translation and protection mechanisms must be manually adapted for each new hardware design, a repetitive and error-prone process that can introduce security-critical bugs breaking isolation guarantees for untrusted applications.
method: Velosiraptor synthesizes correct-by-construction OS memory translation code from a hardware-description specification of the translation/protection hardware. It takes a formal hardware model (specifying translation table formats, field semantics, and configuration operations) as input and automatically generates the OS driver code that correctly configures the hardware. The synthesis process uses a component library of translation operations and a constraint solver or template-based code generator to produce verified, hardware-specific configuration routines without manual coding.

title: RTSpMSpM: Harnessing Ray Tracing for Efficient Sparse Matrix Computations
problem: Sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (SpMSpM) is a critical kernel for graph analytics, GNNs, and scientific computing, but existing GPU SpMSpM libraries underutilize hardware because the irregular memory access and conditional computation patterns of sparse data do not map well to standard GPU CUDA cores and tensor units.
method: The authors first observe the algorithmic analogy between SpMSpM (identifying non-zero output positions) and ray-triangle intersection (finding ray-geometry intersections), then implement SW-RTSpMSpM — an SpMSpM algorithm mapped to the standard ray tracing API (DXR/OptiX) that uses RT core intersection units for non-zero position detection. Analysis of the differences between the two algorithms motivates RT+SpMSpM, which introduces two architectural optimizations: (1) simultaneous computation of partial products alongside RT intersection tests (not just detection), and (2) a ray mapping and scheduling strategy paired with a small row accumulation engine (RAE) that exploits Gustavson's sparse row-by-column dataflow and eliminates reliance on shader fallbacks and redundant memory operations. The RAE introduces only 0.2% area overhead on a modern high-end RT GPU.

title: QuCLEAR: Clifford Extraction and Absorption for Quantum Circuit Optimization
problem: Near-term quantum devices have high gate error rates, and the dominant approach of reducing two-qubit gate count via peephole optimization or routing-aware compilation leaves substantial overhead from Clifford subcircuits that could be eliminated rather than merely rearranged.
method: QuCLEAR is a compilation framework with two sequential optimization steps. First, Clifford Extraction identifies and extracts Clifford subcircuits from the original circuit, commuting them to the end of the circuit via a series of gate commutation rules while simultaneously optimizing (reducing) the remaining non-Clifford gates; this process changes the structure of the remaining circuit to expose further simplifications. Second, Clifford Absorption leverages the classical simulatability of Clifford circuits to compute their effect analytically and absorb (classically post-process) the extracted Clifford subcircuit rather than executing it on quantum hardware, eliminating those gates entirely from the quantum circuit.

title: SparseWeaver: Converting Sparse Operations as Dense Operations on GPUs for Graph Workloads
problem: Real-world graph workloads have sparse and skewed adjacency structures that cause severe warp-level load imbalance on GPUs, where existing software or hardware balancing schemes incur memory overhead or excessive inter- and intra-warp synchronization cost.
method: SparseWeaver is a hardware-software co-design that converts sparse graph operations into balanced dense operations by exploiting graph topology. A lightweight GPU functional unit microarchitecture called Weaver is added to GPU cores; it analyzes common sparse-to-dense conversion patterns identified via static/dynamic analysis and implements the conversion directly in the execution pipeline, leveraging memory access locality without additional synchronization. The design is prototyped on the open-source RISC-V Vortex GPU.

title: Exo 2: Growing a Scheduling Language
problem: User-schedulable languages (USLs) fix a single design point for what programmers control and what is automated, but no universal control/automation split exists even in narrow domains, causing USLs to be inextensible when new hardware targets or optimization strategies emerge.
method: Exo 2 enables users to define new scheduling operations externally to the compiler by composing a set of trusted fine-grained primitives (actions for modifying code, inspection for querying code structure, and references for pointing to code locations). The key mechanism is Cursors, a new abstraction that unifies code references across actions, inspections, and scheduling library composition, allowing safe user-defined scheduling transformations. Users build scheduling libraries that amortize transformation effort across related kernels without modifying the compiler internals.

title: SYLQ-SV: Scaling Symbolic Execution of Hardware Designs with Query Caching
problem: Symbolic execution of hardware designs (in SystemVerilog) suffers from path explosion, making full security and functional verification intractably expensive. Existing engines lack comprehensive SystemVerilog language support and do not exploit redundancy across SMT queries generated during path exploration.
method: SylQ-SV is a dedicated SystemVerilog symbolic execution engine that caches SMT queries across paths. When the engine encounters a query that is semantically equivalent to a previously solved one, it retrieves the cached result rather than re-invoking the SMT solver, avoiding redundant computation. The engine also provides full SystemVerilog language coverage including SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) to support end-to-end verification of open-source designs.

title: KernelGPT: Enhanced Kernel Fuzzing via Large Language Models
problem: Kernel fuzzing effectiveness depends critically on syscall specifications that define the syntax and semantics of system calls, but generating these specifications is largely manual work, leaving large numbers of important syscalls uncovered and limiting automated kernel vulnerability discovery.
method: KernelGPT uses large language models to automatically generate and repair syscall specifications for kernel fuzzing. The system prompts an LLM with kernel source code and documentation to synthesize syscall specifications in the format expected by the Syzkaller fuzzer, then uses an iterative refinement loop where fuzzing feedback is fed back to the LLM to repair invalid or incomplete specifications. This LLM-guided specification generation covers previously uncovered syscalls and improves the semantic validity of generated syscall sequences.
